newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan WTO speech falls on few ears.
newsitem.headline: Japan WTO speech falls on few ears.

text.p: Japan's global trade prestige suffered an embarrassment on Tuesday when few listeners could be found for an address by its foreign minister at this week's gathering of world trade chiefs.

Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda appealed to members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), gathered here for their first ministerial conference, to forge a deal to scrap high-tech tariffs and expand the world trade watchdog's agenda to include the contentious issues of investment and competition policy.
But not many delegates heard the plea.

In sharp contrast to the large audiences which listened on Monday to speeches by a raft of trade chiefs including Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan, only a few delegates turned up to hear Ikeda.

Japan's aspirations to play a high-profile role at the five-day meeting of the multilateral body whose importance Tokyo has long advocated, have already been hampered by the absence of Trade Minister Shinji Sato at this week's gathering.
Sato was forced to stay at home to face questions in parliament about a scandal linking bureaucrats at his ministry to an oil wholesaler arrested on suspicion of tax evasion.

Ikeda's appearance, meanwhile, is set to be brief. He arrived before dawn on Tuesday and was scheduled to leave late in the day, although Japanese officials -- privately embarrassed by Sato's no-show -- said the top diplomat's stay might be extended to Wednesday.
Ikeda has also been constrained by the need to attend parliamentary discussions back home.

Japanese trade negotiators have been putting the best face on the lack of top leadership at the gathering, but one of the political members of the delegation confessed that it was hardly the best of all possible worlds.

"Of course parliament is very important, but at this time of such important negotiations, I did have the feeling that I wanted the minister to come," Seiko Noda, parliamentary vice minister for posts and telecommunications, said on Monday.

Noda, a 36-year-old twice-elected MP, attended informal talks on Monday aimed at boosting momentum to forge a WTO deal on telecommunication services by a February 15 deadline. She did so in place of her minister, also kept at home by parliamentary business.
